newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industrial insurance rates unlikely to rise.
newsitem.headline: German industrial insurance rates unlikely to rise.

text.p: German industrial insurance is unlikely to fetch higher prices for the foreseeable future, German insurance federation Gesamtverband der Deutschen Versicherungswirtschaft (GDV) experts said in Dresden.

"Especially in industrial fire, there is an extremely competitive struggle for market share," Werner Schimming, board member of the Albingia insurance group and chairman of GDV's industrial property insurance committee, said at an industry meeting.
Schimming said 130 companies are currently active in the industrial fire market, including 28 foreign insurers.
"In 1995, the average premium was already the lowest in Europe, at 0.086 percent in fire and 0.096 percent for business interruption. Since then, rates have dropped further," he said.
On the loss side, arson posed a major threat.

"Around 13 percent of all losses are due to arson. In the claims total this runs to 25 percent," Schimming said. "This does not include undiscovered arson." Of warehouse fires, 57 percent were due to arson.
However, insurers still produced a gross underwriting profit in industrial fire during 1996, Schimming said, although it was down from 170 million marks in 1995 to 50 million marks last year.
This was largely the result of settlement profits -- the combined ratio for the year 1996 was 114 percent, against 111 percent in 1995.
In all industrial property lines together, the industry made an underwriting profit of gross 150 million marks, compared with 220 million marks the year before.
"This is a return on turnover of less than two percent, which our industrial customers would consider low," said Schimming.

In industrial liability, the German market posted an underwriting loss of 700 million marks, compared with a 590 million marks loss in 1995. This was largely the result of high reserves for environmental and other liability risks, said liability expert Herbert Schilling of the Gerling group.
All German industrial insurance together recorded premium income of 13.69 billion marks in 1996, a slight decrease on the 13.81 billion marks of 1995.

Of that, 4.0 billion marks came from fire, down from 4.21 billion marks. Extended coverage recorded 0.50 billion, versus 0.47 billion marks. Engineering insurance ran to 2.80 billion marks, largely unchanged on the 2.81 billion marks of 1995.
Marine totalled 1.99 billion, down from 2.06 billion and excluding private lines such as travel luggage insurance.
Industrial liability recorded premium income of 4.40 billion marks, up from 4.25 billion marks.
Combined ratios were 106 percent in engineering after 105 percent and in marine 115 percent after 118 percent.
After settlement profits, gross underwriting profits in engineering went up from 85 million marks to 100 million marks, in marine they improved from a loss of 35 million marks to a break-even result.
